title: Measles cases rise in November despite catch-up vaccination drive
excerpt: Daily cases and admissions in early November are above October's averages. Sylhet reports two more infant deaths, taking its toll to 220.
content:
The measles outbreak is not slowing seven weeks after the government stepped up its catch-up vaccination campaign, according to an analysis of Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) data by The Daily Star. Daily cases and hospital admissions in the first 16 days of November were higher than October's averages.

Key figures

  • November daily average: 1,405 cases and 1,214 admissions, against 1,267 and 1,088 in October (The Daily Star)
  • Daily deaths averaged 4.12 in November, slightly down from 4.65 in October
  • 1,405 admissions in one day, the second-highest since the outbreak began. The highest was 1,415 on 27 July
  • 249,569 people with symptoms and 25,442 confirmed cases since 15 March (bdnews24.com)
  • 19.06 lakh more children vaccinated since 27 September. The campaign first targeted about 34 lakh

In Sylhet, two more infants, aged six months and seven months, died at Jalalabad Ragib Rabeya Medical College Hospital and Osmani Medical College Hospital, bdnews24.com's Bangla edition reported on 17 November. That takes the division's measles death toll to 220, said Mohammad Noore Alam Shamim, assistant director of the Sylhet health department. The division has 1,628 lab-confirmed cases since 1 January.

The DGHS bulletins count only people treated in hospital, so the true number of cases is not known. Reports from the two outlets also give different national death totals, so Devlens is not quoting a single figure until the DGHS publishes a reconciled count.

Why it matters

Babies too young to be fully vaccinated are among those dying, and the catch-up drive has reached just over half of the children it first aimed for. Community health workers, many employed by NGOs, are central to finding missed children and getting sick children to care early. Rising admissions also put pressure on child wards already stretched by dengue.

What to watch

Whether the vaccination campaign is extended or redirected to districts with the most cases, and whether DGHS publishes clearer death figures.
